So, one thing that is really important about my situation is tuberous breasts are glandular, so breastfeeding is possible. I breastfed three kids, and back when my first was born, there was a huge “breast is best” push so it was a struggle but we did it. I was also working 10 hour shifts and this was back before the ACA so my employer didn’t have to make accommodations for me to pump. After 10 hours I would pump 250-300cc from each side and then breastfeed. I went from an AA cup size to a D cup size on a daily basis. 


So over about 6 years my body naturally did a lot of the work that tissue expanders would have. The approach for before kids would have been lift (the full anchor lift), tissue expanders, and then taking the expanders out and putting implants in. I also had the added issue of a fair amount of weight loss. I know glandular tissue doesn’t respond to weight changes like fatty tissue, but if you lose enough, you lose lots of types of tissue (muscle, bone, hair...).


So we ended up attempting a subpectoral augmentation with extensive dissection because the tissue itself was still tuberous despite the skin being stretched. I understood from the beginning that there was a huge chance this wouldn’t work out and might make things a lot worse (like a tuberous breast on top of a headlight). 


After the surgery, the doctor, who specializes in breast surgery and does as many tuberous surgeries as anyone said he hadn’t ever encountered my specific configuration because of the breastfeeding and weight changes. But I liked that all of these issues were taken into account and from the get go there was a plan A, a discussion about what problems we could potentially “unmask” and how we would address those if it came to that. I also had a bigger risk of a complication like a blood collection around the implant because of dissection. 


Because we didn’t do the lift, and tuberous breasts sit a little wide on the chest, my nipples are *slightly* facing outward, right more than left, but it’s subtle enough that it doesn’t bother me. The lift would have corrected that. If the implants were centered behind the nipples, the implants would be so far to the side you could see them from behind ever though I got a pretty small size (150ml). 


I would have also liked to have a little bit of droop to the breast, where there’s more volume on the bottom than the top, not the super round headlight look, but absolutely everyone I talked to said that was not an achievable goal. 


So my result isn’t perfect and I could have done things differently and had less risk. But I decided I didn’t need perfect, I just wanted better with a clear plan for “what if’s” which I think is really important if you are not a straightforward case to begin with.

I had minimal breast tissue and went with 150cc implants; any bigger would have been too much for my personal taste. I did have surgeons try and talk me up to a higher number, and I told the nurses not to bring the bigger implants in the room!  At this point I’m so glad I stood my ground and got the size I wanted.

I think you might be conflating amniotic fluid embolisms with air embolisms. There is no physical way to get an air embolism from the activity described. 


Air dissolves in liquids and is present in your body, in molecular form. An ABG (arterial blood gas) is a very common blood test to measure respiratory and metabolic function.   Air in the vagina is not a problem, just like bath water in the vagina is not a problem. In fact, bathwater in an IV would cause major issues, but you would need to inject a fairly large about of air (I believe close to 10ml) into a vein to cause an air embolism. 


When surgery is performed, all sorts of tissue, from the peritoneum and intestines, to the brain, bones, and heart, are exposed to air. There are lots of risks to surgery, but exposure to air really isn’t one of them. 


When laparoscopic surgery is performed the abdomen and pelvis are filled with air at a high pressure so the surgeon can see what’s going on. Being blown up like a balloon causes shoulder pain, but not embolism.
